kjv-italics-revision.d: Open a King James Bible. Some words are printed in italics. Those are words the 1611 translators added to make the English read smoothly. They are not in the Hebrew.
Nobody translating from ancient gold plates could know which English words a 1611 committee had added. Those words exist only in that one edition.

kjv-italics-revision.t: What the Book of Mormon does
kjv-italics-revision.d: It quotes long stretches of Isaiah. Where its wording differs from the King James, the changes cluster on exactly those italic words. David Wright counted it: between 22% and 38% of the differences land there. And about 40% of the italic words are simply dropped.

Stan Spencer of the Interpreter Foundation accepts the pattern. He argues Joseph Smith could see the italics on the page, treated them as suspect, and revised around them while dictating. That is a real answer, and it fits the data.
It concedes he was working from a King James Bible. That is the whole point at issue.
"Why would a translation from gold plates track the italics of one English edition?"

deutero-isaiah-problem.d: Most scholars think Isaiah 40-55 had a second, unnamed author. They date it to about 545 BC, during the exile in Babylon. Two reasons. Those chapters treat the exile as already happening. And they name Cyrus, a Persian king who had not been born in Isaiah's day.

deutero-isaiah-problem.t: Why that is a problem here
deutero-isaiah-problem.d: Lehi left Jerusalem around 600 BC, before the exile. So those chapters could not have been on the brass plates he carried. Yet Nephi, Jacob and Abinadi all quote them at length.

Two lines. Kevin Barney and FAIR accept the late dating. They suggest the wording entered during translation — Joseph putting Nephite ideas into the King James Isaiah he knew. Others reject the dating and defend one Isaiah in the 700s BC.

Strong for you. The first answer concedes that part of the text is not ancient. The second requires overturning two centuries of scholarship — which some conservatives do attempt, and you should say so.
"If those chapters were written after Lehi left, how were they on his plates?"

another-gospel-canon-closure.t: The two verses Christians reach for
another-gospel-canon-closure.d: Galatians 1:8 — "though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you… let him be accursed" — applied to the angel Moroni. And Revelation 22:18, warning against adding to the book.

another-gospel-canon-closure.t: Be careful with the second one
another-gospel-canon-closure.d: Revelation 22:18 says "the words of the prophecy of this book." That means Revelation itself. It is a standard closing curse for one ancient scroll. Revelation was not even the last book of the New Testament written. Using it to shut the whole Bible is bad reading, and your friend will say so.

another-gospel-canon-closure.t: Where the first verse does work
another-gospel-canon-closure.d: Galatians 1:8 is different. It does not say an angel cannot appear. It grants the possibility and removes its authority: the message is tested by the gospel already delivered. And Paul includes himself — though we — which makes it a test rather than a weapon.
Arguable both ways. The canon half fails. The Galatians half holds — and it holds against us too.
"I'd have to reject an angel with a new gospel too. Paul puts himself under that rule."

grace-after-all-we-can-do.d: 2 Nephi 25:23 — "it is by grace that we are saved, after all we can do." Moroni 10:32 adds: deny yourselves of all ungodliness, then is his grace sufficient.
It reads like a condition. Your own maximum effort first, then God covers the gap. Ephesians 2:8-9 says the opposite — saved by grace through faith, "not of works, lest any man should boast."

Stephen Robinson of BYU says "after all we can do" is an old turn of phrase. He reads it as in spite of all we can do. And in 2015 Dieter Uchtdorf, of the First Presidency, preached grace in words most evangelicals would recognise.

Arguable both ways. The old-phrase reading is fair. The modern preaching is real. But ask what the system asks of a member in practice. Temple worthiness. Interviews. Ordinances. Then see if that matches the sermon.
"When you stand before God, what are you resting on?"

trinitarian-monotheism-1830.t: What the Book of Mormon says about God
trinitarian-monotheism-1830.d: It is strictly monotheistic, and the Father-Son unity is so tight it reads almost as one person in two roles. Mosiah 15:1-5 has Christ as "the Father and the Son… one God." Alma 11:26-29 says there is one God and no other.
That the Father, Son and Holy Ghost are three separate beings. That the Father has a body of flesh and bone. And that faithful people may become gods themselves.

David Paulsen of BYU says the 1830 text read whole is not modalist. It does tell Father and Son apart in other places. He adds that early Christian writers were loose with words too, before the councils tightened them.
Arguable on any one verse. Harder to argue with is the direction of travel. The 1830 book sounds much more like ordinary Christianity than 1844 does.
"Read me Alma 11:26-29 in your own book. How many Gods does it say there are?"

1837-son-of-edits.d: 1 Nephi 11:18 called Mary "the mother of God." 11:21 called Jesus "the Lamb of God, yea, even the Eternal Father." 13:40 said "the Lamb of God is the Eternal Father."
Joseph Smith inserted the words the Son of. Mary became the mother of the Son of God. The Lamb became the Son of the Eternal Father. The change is small and it is not accidental.
FAIR says a translator may clarify his own work. Royal Skousen treats the change as clarifying, not correcting. Both readings work, they say, since Christ is called Eternal Father in the book anyway.
Arguable. But watch the timing. The edits land just as the teaching about God moves from one being to three separate ones.
"Why did those four verses need the words 'the Son of' added in 1837?"

jacob-polygamy-vs-dc132.t: What the Book of Mormon says
jacob-polygamy-vs-dc132.d: Jacob 2:24 says David's and Solomon's many wives were "abominable before me, saith the Lord." Verse 27 commands: "there shall not any man among you have save it be one wife; and concubines he shall have none."
That David's wives and concubines "were given unto him of me." The same practice, from the same God, with the opposite verdict.
FAIR points to Jacob 2:30, which they read as an exception clause: monogamy is the rule, unless God commands otherwise to raise up seed. That reading is available in the text.
Here the Bible and the Book of Mormon agree with each other, and D&C 132 stands alone against both. That is worth pointing out gently.
"Your own scripture calls it abominable. What changed?"

unchangeable-god-vs-king-follett.t: What the Book of Mormon says
unchangeable-god-vs-king-follett.d: Moroni 8:18 — God is "unchangeable from all eternity to all eternity." That matches the Bible: Psalm 90:2, Malachi 3:6, and Isaiah 43:10, where God says "before me there was no God formed."
In 1844 he preached at a funeral for a man named King Follett. He taught that God "was once as we are now" — a man who rose to become God. And that we may do the same.

Blake Ostler and FAIR argue Moroni 8:18 is about God's character — he is not fickle or partial — rather than his history. The surrounding verses are about God's fairness to children, which supports that reading.
Strong for you. The character reading is fair for Moroni 8:18 on its own. It does not help with Isaiah 43:10, which is about existence, not temperament.
"Read me Isaiah 43:10. Was there ever a God before this one?"

no-postmortem-repentance.t: What the Book of Mormon says
no-postmortem-repentance.d: Alma 34:32-35: "this life is the time for men to prepare to meet God," and after it comes "the night of darkness wherein there can be no labor performed." Those who put off repentance are sealed to the devil — "this is the final state of the wicked."
The spirit world, where the gospel is preached to the dead, and baptism performed by proxy for them by the living.

That Amulek is addressing the Zoramites — people who had already received the gospel and rejected it. His warning applies to them, not to the billions who never heard. D&C 138 makes that distinction explicit.
Genuinely arguable. The Zoramite context is real. But Alma's language is sweeping, and the Bible says the same thing in Hebrews 9:27.
"Alma says there's no labour after this life. How does that fit with baptism for the dead?"

born-at-jerusalem.d: Alma 7:10 prophesies that Jesus "shall be born of Mary, at Jerusalem which is the land of our forefathers." The Bible says Bethlehem — Micah 5:2 predicts it, Matthew 2 and Luke 2 report it.

And this one is good. The verse says the land of our fathers, not the city. The Book of Mormon uses "the land of Jerusalem" more than forty times for the whole region. Bethlehem is five miles away. An Egyptian letter from the 1300s BC even calls Bethlehem part of the land of Jerusalem.
Genuinely arguable, and this is one where the Latter-day Saint answer is stronger than most critics admit. Do not lead with it.
Give away a weak argument openly and you earn a hearing on the strong ones. The papyri. The italics. The Isaiah dating.
"I've heard this one used against you and I don't think it works. Can I ask about something that does?"

plain-precious-things-removed.t: The claim that makes a restoration necessary
plain-precious-things-removed.d: 1 Nephi 13 says a "great and abominable church" deliberately took from the gospel "many parts which are plain and most precious, and also many covenants." If the Bible was gutted, something has to replace it.
Because we have the copies. Thousands of them, from before and across that whole span. In Greek, Latin, Syriac and Coptic. Made in places that never spoke to each other.
No sign of a coordinated removal. Variants exist and are catalogued, but they are spelling, word order, and a handful of footnoted passages. Nothing doctrine rests on.

FAIR and Scripture Central move the loss earlier — to the first or second century, before our oldest full copies. If it happened then, the copies could not show it. That is a real answer. It is also one that no evidence could ever count against.
"If it was removed before our oldest copies, what evidence could ever count either way?"

no-nephite-material-culture.d: Cities. Temples. Roads. Coins. Steel swords and armour. Civilizations in the millions. And a final battle with hundreds of thousands of dead.
After about 190 years of digging in the Americas: not one city. Not one battlefield, road, temple or skeleton tied to the book. No inscription. And no site the church itself points to.

John Sorenson keeps the whole story inside a corridor of about 500 miles in Central America. If that is right, an empty hemisphere proves nothing. He lists hundreds of claimed matches with Maya culture.

The church takes no official position on where it happened. And the small-map idea is a long way from what was taught for a century. Back then, the Lamanites were the ancestors of all American Indians.
"Where did it happen? I'd genuinely like to read the church's position on that."

translation-seer-stone.d: Joseph Smith reading from gold plates, perhaps with a curtain, writing down what he read. That is what church manuals and paintings showed for about 150 years.

Something different. He put a brown stone into his hat, buried his face in it to block the light, and dictated. The plates were often covered, or in another room, or not there at all. That comes from Emma Smith, David Whitmer and Martin Harris — insiders, not critics.
He had used the same stone earlier for treasure-seeking, which is what brought him before a court in 1826.

This one has a clear answer — the church now teaches it openly. The Gospel Topics essay says so, the Joseph Smith Papers document it, and the church published photographs of the stone in 2015. The scandal was the silence, not the stone.
"Have you seen the church's photos of the seer stone? What did you picture before that?"

lost-116-pages.d: In 1828 Martin Harris borrowed the first 116 pages of the translation and lost them. They were never recovered.

They were not retranslated. A revelation, now D&C 10, said wicked men had altered the lost pages and would publish the altered version to discredit him. So he was told to translate a different set of plates covering the same period instead.

That this is guarding against forgery, not dodging. Dictated translation never comes out word for word the same twice. If enemies held the only other copy, any difference would be paraded as proof he made it up.
Arguable. The forgery worry is reasonable. What is worth noticing is that a replacement text already existed, covering the same years. And no altered version was ever published.
"Did the altered pages ever actually appear?"

witnesses-character-and-vision.d: Eleven men signed statements printed in the front of every Book of Mormon. Three describe an angel and a voice; eight describe handling the plates. It is the strongest evidence the book has, and it deserves serious treatment.

witnesses-character-and-vision.t: What is worth knowing about them
witnesses-character-and-vision.d: All eleven were Smith family, Whitmer family, or Martin Harris. None was an outsider. And all of them lived in a world where seeing by "second sight" was normal.

witnesses-character-and-vision.t: How some of them described it
witnesses-character-and-vision.d: Harris spoke of seeing "with the eyes of faith" and "spiritual eyes." Stephen Burnett's 1838 letter reports Harris saying so publicly.

witnesses-character-and-vision.t: Their answer, and it is strong
witnesses-character-and-vision.d: Not one of the eleven ever took it back. Not Cowdery. Not Harris. Not Whitmer — even after being thrown out of the church, when taking it back would have cost nothing. Whitmer never came back to the church, and reaffirmed it as he was dying.
Genuinely arguable, and this is the best card the other side holds. Treat it with respect.
"What do you make of the 'spiritual eyes' language? I'm asking honestly."

gold-plates-never-examined.d: The plates were shown only to people Joseph Smith chose. Family. Money backers. Early believers. Then they were returned to the angel. No scholar or neutral party ever saw them, and none ever can.

gold-plates-never-examined.t: What that does and does not mean
gold-plates-never-examined.d: It is not proof of anything on its own. Plenty of genuine ancient objects are lost. But it does mean the central physical evidence for the book is permanently unavailable for testing.

An interesting one. Witnesses put the plates at 40 to 60 pounds. Solid gold that size would weigh about 200. But tumbaga is different — a copper-gold mix used in Central America, gilded on the surface. Plates that size in tumbaga would weigh about 53 to 58 pounds, and look like gold. That fits a real object better than a forger would have guessed.
Strong for you on the main point, but give them the tumbaga argument first. It is a good one, and pretending otherwise costs you.
"Is there anything that could be examined today, either way?"

kinderhook-plates.d: In 1843 three men in Illinois made six small brass plates. They covered them in made-up "ancient" writing, buried them in a mound, and brought them to Joseph Smith. The point was to see whether he would translate them.

His clerk William Clayton recorded that Smith said the plates contained the history of a descendant of Ham. The plates were later proved a hoax; one of the makers admitted it, and metal testing in 1980 confirmed a nineteenth-century origin.

And the church's own published position agrees with much of it. Smith never produced a translation. He never claimed revelation about them. Don Bradley and Mark Ashurst-McGee argue he was trying a scholarly comparison, using his Egyptian alphabet papers.
This one has a clear answer, and the answer goes largely their way. Clayton's entry is secondhand, and no translation exists. Use it as evidence about method, not as a knockout.
"What do you make of the Kinderhook episode? I've read the church's account of it."

source-parallels-voth-late-war.t: Two books that were around before 1830
source-parallels-voth-late-war.d: Ethan Smith's View of the Hebrews (1823) argued American Indians descended from the lost tribes of Israel. It was published in the town where Oliver Cowdery's family lived. And Gilbert Hunt's The Late War (1816) retold the War of 1812 in King James English for schoolchildren.

B. H. Roberts, a senior Latter-day Saint leader and historian, privately compiled a 291-page study listing about 26 structural similarities with View of the Hebrews — a divided people, a buried record, and more.

Roberts drew no conclusion of dependence. He framed the work as questions a believer must be able to answer, and he died affirming the Book of Mormon. Using him as a witness for the prosecution misrepresents what he said.
Genuinely arguable. Parallels are easy to find and easy to overstate. The honest version is narrow: these ideas were in the air, in that region, in that decade.
"Have you read what B. H. Roberts actually wrote? He was one of yours."

book-of-abraham-papyri.t: Why this case is different from all the others
book-of-abraham-papyri.d: The source document survives. For the Book of Mormon the plates are gone. Here, we have the papyri.

In 1835 Joseph Smith bought Egyptian papyri from a travelling mummy exhibition. He declared one roll to be "the writings of Abraham while he was in Egypt" and published the Book of Abraham in 1842. The papyri were thought lost, then rediscovered in 1966.

book-of-abraham-papyri.t: What they turned out to be
book-of-abraham-papyri.d: Ordinary Egyptian funeral texts — a Book of Breathings made for a Theban priest named Hor, from around the second century BC. That is roughly 1,500 years after Abraham. Every Egyptologist who has examined them agrees, including Latter-day Saint ones.

Two defences, both in the church's own essay. The missing-scroll idea says the surviving pieces are a small remnant, and the Abraham text was on a lost part. The catalyst idea says the papyri simply prompted revelation, and the text was never a translation at all.
Strong for you — this is the single most testable claim in the whole section. But note what the catalyst theory concedes: that the words are not on the papyri at all.
"The church says Egyptologists read these differently than he did. What do you make of that?"

stylometry-wordprint-studies.d: Writers have measurable habits — how often they use small words like of and and. Statisticians have tried to use those fingerprints to work out who wrote the Book of Mormon.

BYU studies by Larsen, Rencher and Layton (1980) and Hilton (1990) found the book's internal narrators are statistically distinguishable from each other and from Joseph Smith. Jockers, Witten and Criddle (2008) pointed instead toward Sidney Rigdon and Solomon Spalding.

BYU statistician Bruce Schaalje identified it. The Jockers method is a closed-set classifier: it is mathematically obliged to assign every chapter to one of the candidates you feed it. If the real author is not on the list, it will still return a confident answer.
Genuinely arguable, and honestly neither side settles anything. Do not cite either study as proof — the method is contested enough that both results should be held loosely.
Nothing. This is a case to know about so you don't get caught using it.

jst-genesis-50-choice-seer.t: What Joseph Smith added to Genesis
jst-genesis-50-choice-seer.d: He produced a revision of the whole Bible. In his version, Genesis 50 gains about fourteen verses in which the dying Joseph of Egypt prophesies a latter-day "choice seer" who will be named Joseph — and whose father will also be named Joseph.
Joseph Smith Jr., son of Joseph Smith Sr.
Nothing like it. Not the Hebrew, not the Dead Sea Scrolls, not the Greek, not the Samaritan text. No ancient copy of Genesis has these verses.

Robert Matthews and Kent Jackson agree that no manuscript has the passage. They argue the revision was never meant to be pure restoration of lost text. It could be new revelation, or inspired comment, added to the page.
Strong for you. That answer is honest, and it concedes the point: a prophecy naming the translator was inserted into Genesis by the translator.
"Which ancient manuscript has those verses in Genesis 50?"

angel-nephi-moroni-name-change.d: Every Latter-day Saint knows him as Moroni — the last Nephite, who buried the plates and returned as an angel to reveal them.

Joseph Smith's official history, published in the Times and Seasons in April 1842 under his own editorship, names the angel Nephi. So does the Millennial Star the same year, the first edition of the Pearl of Great Price in 1851, and Lucy Mack Smith's 1853 history.

FAIR and church historians call it a copying slip. They say clerks introduced it while compiling the 1838-39 history. And they point to earlier sources that already say Moroni — Oliver Cowdery's letters from 1835.
Genuinely arguable. A clerical error is entirely possible. What makes it worth knowing is that the error survived into published scripture and stood for years.
"Have you seen the 1842 Times and Seasons? It names the angel Nephi."

first-vision-multiple-accounts.d: God the Father and Jesus Christ appearing to Joseph Smith in a grove of trees. Everything else rests on it.

first-vision-multiple-accounts.t: He told it more than once
first-vision-multiple-accounts.d: At least four times in his own lifetime, and the accounts differ. The 1832 one is in his own handwriting. It describes one person, not two. It gives his age as about fifteen or sixteen. And it says he had already decided the churches were wrong before he prayed. The 1838 account — the one now in scripture — has two persons and a different order of events.

The church's own Gospel Topics essay acknowledges all the accounts. It argues the differences reflect audience, purpose and memory rather than invention: the 1832 telling is about personal forgiveness, the 1838 about which church to join.

Genuinely arguable. People do retell formative experiences differently. What is harder is that the number of persons present changes, and that most members never heard there was more than one account.
"Have you read the 1832 account in his own hand? The church published it."

first-vision-revival-dating.d: That there was an "unusual excitement on the subject of religion" in the Palmyra area in 1820, which added "great multitudes" to the churches, and that this is what sent him to pray.

Wesley Walters went looking in 1967. He examined Presbyterian, Methodist and Baptist records for Palmyra and found no significant revival in 1820. The major local revival was in 1824-25 — after the date given.

Milton Backman replied in 1969, documenting Methodist camp meetings near Palmyra in 1819-20 and revival activity across the wider Genesee region. "In that region of country" is a loose phrase and need not mean Palmyra alone.
Genuinely arguable. Backman's reply is real and should be given. But the account describes multitudes joining churches locally, and the membership numbers for those years do not show it.
"When was the big revival in Palmyra? It's worth checking the church records."

word-of-wisdom-dietary-law.d: D&C 89, given in 1833. It counsels against wine, strong drink, tobacco and "hot drinks" — later defined as coffee and tea. Its own second verse says it is sent "not by commandment or constraint."
Under Heber J. Grant, keeping it became a fixed requirement for a temple recommend, formalised by about 1921. So a cup of coffee can now keep a member out of the temple, and out of a child's wedding.
That it is a health code and a covenant standard, not a purity law — the body as a temple, as in 1 Corinthians 6:19-20. A church may raise a standard over time without contradicting itself.
Arguable both ways. The real question is not coffee. It is what happens when advice given expressly not as a commandment becomes a test of worthiness. That is close to what Jesus rebuked in Mark 7.
"D&C 89:2 says it isn't a commandment. When did that change, and who changed it?"

temple-garments-practice.d: Endowed members covenant to wear the temple garment — prescribed white underclothing bearing sacred marks. The General Handbook instructs that it be worn "day and night throughout your life" and never altered. Since 2024 the recommend interview includes a standard statement about it.
Do not mock it. "Magic underwear" is the single fastest way to end the conversation, and it deserves to end. This is sacred to the person in front of you and it is personal.
That it is a private reminder of covenants made in the temple — no stranger than a nun's habit, a priest's collar, a Jewish prayer shawl or a Muslim skullcap. That comparison is fair.
Not whether clothing can be sacred — plainly it can. Whether daily clothing should be a condition of standing before God, and where Scripture prescribes that for ordinary believers.
"I'm not going to make fun of it. Can I ask what it means to you?"
